clue.text: Where there's muck there's brass — for such people?

definitions.text: Where there's muck there's brass — for such people?

parts.words: Where there's muck there's brass — for such people?
parts.note: the proverb links dirt with money; read literally, people who reek of muck and are loaded with brass (money) are both foul-smelling and wealthy

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire proverb about dirty work paying well, asked of the people it describes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muck' gives the smelly first word and 'brass', northern English slang for money, gives the second; the slang phrase for very wealthy is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for extremely wealthy, and the proverb says money comes from dirty trades.

clue.text: Nurse is working when it's getting light

indicators.note: something working is in operation, so these letters are set to work in a new order

explanation.surface: A nurse on the early shift is at work as dawn breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges NURSE IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Daybreak is the time when the sky starts to brighten.

clue.text: Dope in Foreign Office

parts.note: taken as written; that the answer also runs across 'in Foreign' is a coincidence, since the setter builds it from in plus the abbreviation
FO is the abbreviation for the British Foreign Office

explanation.surface: Inside information leaking from the British diplomatic ministry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' here is slang for inside information, not a drug or a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is informal for facts or details, and the short form of information means the same.

clue.text: Monarch conceals evil crime

indicators.note: the monarch's word hides another word within it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a monarch is a king
ill means evil or harm, as in 'speak ill of'

explanation.surface: A ruler covers up a wicked offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evil' looks like an adjective on 'crime', but it is the word inside; 'conceals' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A murder is the gravest crime, and the word is a common synonym for a slaying.

clue.text: Playing note was easy-peasy

indicators.note: playing about with letters, as a musician plays a piece, signals they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A musician says that playing the note was no trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' rearranges NOTE WAS. The phrase is informal for no trouble at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal ways of saying a task was simple and caused no difficulty.

clue.text: Authentic-sounding piece of film

indicators.note: '-sounding' tells us the word for authentic is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: authentic means real or genuine

explanation.surface: A genuine-seeming fragment of film footage.
explanation.walkthrough: '-sounding' gives a word pronounced like REAL but spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A reel is a spool holding a length of cinema film, and by extension the film on it.

clue.text: Blooming band beginning to play in wooden building

indicators.note: the first letter is placed inside the building word

parts.note: a chalet is a wooden house, typically in the Alps

indicators.note: the beginning of the word play means its first letter

explanation.surface: A band starts a gig in a log cabin and is a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming band' looks like a successful group of musicians; it is a ring of flowers. 'beginning to' takes P from 'play', and 'in' puts it inside CHALET.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a garland or wreath of flowers worn on the head.

clue.text: Unsure how to proceed, with no more jokes to tell?

definitions.text: with no more jokes to tell?

explanation.surface: A comedian who has run out of material and does not know what to do next.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes 'wits' as jokes or witticisms, so their end means none are left.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means baffled and helpless; literally, a joker whose supply of witty remarks has run out.

clue.text: Re establishing relations like gardener after a gale?

explanation.surface: Making peace with neighbours, or repairing the garden after a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for patching up a relationship is read literally as repairing storm-damaged fences.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means restoring friendly terms after a quarrel; literally, a gardener repairing panels blown down by wind.

clue.text: In fun, talk about gas supply?

indicators.note: the letters are moved about, so the words fun and talk are mixed up

explanation.surface: A joking chat about a supply of gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges FUN TALK. 'Gas' is American for petrol, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A full tank's worth of petrol, called gas in the US, is a supply of fuel.

clue.text: Instruction referring reader to leak?

explanation.surface: A footnote directing a reader to an article about a leak.
explanation.walkthrough: Split in two, the answer is a cross-reference such as 'see page 12'; whole, it is a slow leak.
explanation.definitionFit: A book's cross-reference tells readers to look at another sheet; seepage is liquid escaping slowly.

clue.text: New story made up about man

indicators.note: turned about, the word for a made-up story reads backwards

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story

explanation.surface: A fresh story was invented concerning a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man' in crosswords can stand for any male first name. 'about' is the reversal signal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil is a man's first name, and crosswords use 'man' to signal any male name.

clue.text: Making use of computers could make you tense

explanation.surface: Working with computers all day can leave you on edge.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is connected to a network; the other is informal for nervy and keyed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Wired describes something linked up electronically, and also slang for edgy or overexcited.

clue.text: Power given to corrupt old copper

parts.note: P is the symbol for power in physics

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or distorted, so the letters of old are rearranged

explanation.surface: A veteran police officer is bribed to go bent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrupt' rearranges OLD to LOD. PLOD is British slang for the police (from Mr Plod, a policeman in children's books).
explanation.definitionFit: Copper and plod are both British slang words for a police officer.

clue.text: Merry, having imbibed American wine

indicators.note: drinking something takes it inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: gay in its older sense means merry or cheerful

explanation.surface: Tipsy after drinking a US vintage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merry' uses the older sense of gay; 'having imbibed' signals the container, fitting the drinking surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamay is a red grape variety and the wine made from it, notably Beaujolais.

clue.text: Dark brown, mostly, added to blue

indicators.note: the second piece is joined on after the first
mostly means most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown colour
the sky is often called the blue

explanation.surface: A dark shade made by mixing brown with blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark brown' looks like one colour, but 'Dark' alone is the definition. 'mostly' cuts the last letter from the brown word; 'added to' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusky means shadowy or dark-skinned, as at twilight.

clue.text: Female hit hard by affair

parts.note: she is the female pronoun
to bang is to strike loudly and hard

explanation.surface: A woman is devastated by a love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affair' looks like a romance, but here means a business or matter, as in 'the whole shebang'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shebang means an affair or matter, used mainly in the phrase for everything involved.

clue.text: Mocking remark about a town in Somerset

parts.note: a taunt is a jeering or mocking remark
on means about, as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: A jibe aimed at a West Country town.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is a county in south-west England; TAUNTON is its county town.
explanation.definitionFit: Taunton is the county town of the south-west English county.

clue.text: Prime Minister, one overturning every charge

indicators.note: the Prime Minister's letters and the one are flipped over, reading backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
each means every

explanation.surface: A premier upsets everyone and is hit with a formal accusation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one overturning' reads as a person, but 'overturning' flips the Prime Minister abbreviation and one together.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach is to bring a formal accusation of misconduct against an official.

clue.text: Coach currently popular writer

explanation.surface: A trainer who is also a fashionable author.
explanation.walkthrough: A Pullman is a luxury railway carriage; Philip Pullman is the bestselling author of His Dark Materials.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pullman is a comfortable railway carriage, and Philip Pullman is a widely read British novelist.

clue.text: Spiteful woman likely to be chased by Cerberus?

definitions.text: likely to be chased by Cerberus?

explanation.surface: A nasty woman being pursued by a monstrous dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Cerberus is the three-headed dog guarding Hades in Greek myth; a cat in the underworld would be the one he chases.
explanation.definitionFit: A hellcat is a fierce, bad-tempered woman; literally a feline of the underworld, fit prey for its guard dog.

clue.text: Imitate what a stripper might do?

explanation.surface: Mimicking a striptease act.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is to mimic someone; the other is to remove clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to impersonate them; a stripper removes garments.

clue.text: Excited humanist, heading off, gives big wave

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters are rearranged
the heading, or first letter, of the word is taken off

explanation.surface: An agitated humanist sets off a huge wave of feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' drops the H of HUMANIST, and 'Excited' rearranges the remaining UMANIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is a huge sea wave caused by an earthquake or eruption.

clue.text: Writer involved in struggle out east over book

indicators.note: being involved in something puts one piece inside the other
in a down clue, over means the word is turned upwards, reading backwards

parts.note: sumo is a Japanese form of wrestling, a struggle from the Far East
a nib is the writing point of a pen

explanation.surface: An author caught up in an Eastern fight over a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out east' points to Japan, home of the wrestling; 'over' is the down-clue reversal signal and 'involved in' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is a single volume collecting several works, so a kind of book.

clue.text: Sailor appears regularly in scarlet

indicators.note: taking every other letter of scarlet means its letters appear at regular intervals

explanation.surface: A seaman turns up now and then dressed in red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears regularly' takes the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of SCARLET.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt is an experienced seaman, so salt alone means a sailor.

clue.text: Left during mid-afternoon meal

indicators.note: during means within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: four o'clock is the middle of the afternoon

explanation.surface: Someone left in the middle of an afternoon meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meal' is not food eaten but ground grain. 'during' puts L inside FOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Meal is coarsely ground grain, and flour is the finely ground kind.

clue.text: Soon principal character leaves opera

indicators.note: the principal, or first, character of the word is dropped

parts.note: Manon is an opera by Massenet

explanation.surface: The lead singer is soon to quit the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principal character' looks like the lead role; it is the first letter, M, of MANON.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old word meaning shortly or in a little while.

clue.text: Landed gentry have the advantage

indicators.note: the words have the letters inside them, running across the join

explanation.surface: The landed gentry hold the upper hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have' signals letters held within LANDED GENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the edge over someone means holding a slight advantage.

clue.text: Adequate punishment

explanation.surface: A penalty that is just about acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is all right or satisfactory; the other is a money penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine means satisfactory or acceptable, and also a sum paid as a penalty.

clue.text: No coat protects girl moving from place to place

indicators.note: the coat word wraps round and shields the girl's name, which goes inside

parts.note: a mac is a raincoat, short for mackintosh
Di is a girl's name, short for Diana

explanation.surface: Without a raincoat, a wandering girl has no protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No coat' looks like a phrase about being unprotected; the No is simply its own letters, and 'protects' wraps the coat round the girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomadic describes people who wander rather than settle in one place.

clue.text: With this my competence is questioned — nice!

definitions.text: With this my competence is questioned

explanation.surface: A self-doubting person asks whether they are up to the job, and is pleasant about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as AM I ABLE, the word asks whether the speaker is competent.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiable means friendly and pleasant; split up, it asks whether the speaker has the ability.

clue.text: Record one new version of Tears without people like Ken Dodd?

parts.note: to enter is to record, as in a ledger

indicators.note: a version of the word Tears, with the two letters added, is a rearrangement of them

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A cover of a sad song, performed without any comedians.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Dodd was a famous British comedian and singer whose 1965 hit was 'Tears'. 'version of' rearranges the letters; 'without' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken Dodd was a comedian and singer, an example of a professional performer who amuses audiences.
